expected_prisoner.name: Anna Burlak
expected_prisoner.description:
Anna Burlak was a leader of the National Textile Workers Union and the Young Pioneers when she was arrested in the 1929 red raid on a May-Day meeting of the Ukrainian Workingmen's Association at Bethlehem, Pennsylvania and held under $5,000 bail on a sedition charge. She went on to a long career as a communist labor organizer in the New England textile mills.

Anna Burlak was an eighteen-year-old silk weaver known as "the Red Flame."

expected_cases.charges: Sedition (1929 raid on a May Day meeting, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania)
expected_cases.sentence: Held under \$5,000 bail on the sedition charge.

case.charges: Attempting to incite insurrection under Georgia’s insurrection statute (Atlanta Six prosecution).
case.sentence: Pretrial detention in Fulton Tower Prison, Atlanta, in the Atlanta Six prosecution, which carried a possible death penalty. Released on $4,000 bail, according to her first-person account published in Labor Defender, August 1930. This was detention pending prosecution, not a death sentence or conviction. The exact physical release date and measured time served remain unverified. Sources: https://revolutionsnewsstand.com/2025/04/05/76326/ ; https://www.cpusa.org/article/anne-burlak-the-red-flame/

operations.name: M. H. Powers

expected.name: M. H. Powers
expected.description: M. H. Powers was a Trade Union Unity League iron-workers' organizer and Communist district organizer from St. Paul, Minnesota. M. H. Powers was jailed in March 1930 for leaflets and a mass meeting of the unemployed and held on the insurrection charge in a death cell. In the spring of 1930 the state of Georgia revived an 1861 anti-slave-insurrection statute to charge a group of Communist and labor organizers with "attempting to incite insurrection" — a capital offense — for organizing Black and white workers into the same unions and leading demonstrations of Atlanta's unemployed. Held without bail in the Fulton Tower Prison and threatened with the electric chair, the "Atlanta Six" became one of the ILD's signature free-speech defenses; the insurrection charges were eventually beaten.

operations.name: Joe Carr

expected.name: Joe Carr
expected.description: Joe Carr was a young West Virginia coal miner and Young Communist League organizer. He began mining at eleven, was the eldest of nine children, and joined the league in September 1928. After training in Cleveland, he went to Atlanta to organize workers. Police arrested Carr and M. H. Powers at a meeting on March 9, 1930. Released and then rearrested when they returned to the meeting, they were held on disorderly-conduct and speaking charges. The prosecution subsequently invoked Georgia's insurrection law against Carr, Powers and four other organizers. Carr was held in Fulton Tower's death cells while the International Labor Defense campaigned for the Atlanta Six.
